info.title: Acme Commerce API
info.summary: Internal ecommerce platform API for catalog, inventory, orders, and fulfillment.
info.description:
Acme Commerce is a fictional ecommerce platform whose APIs are the product. This document
describes the internal API used by first-party applications.

## Conventions

**Envelopes.** A single resource is `{ "data": { ... } }`. A paginated collection is
`{ "data": [ ... ], "pagination": { ... } }`. Every error is
`{ "error": { "code", "message", "request_id", "details"? } }`. Wrapping leaves room to add
metadata later without breaking existing clients.

The platform endpoints `/health`, `/ready`, and `/openapi.json` sit outside that envelope
and outside the version prefix, deliberately: they describe the process, not the product, and
a container probe should not have to track API versions.

**Field naming.** `snake_case` in JSON, everywhere, in both directions.

**Money.** Integer minor units with a separate currency — `price_cents: 12900` with
`currency: "CAD"` means CAD 129.00. Never a float: IEEE-754 cannot represent 0.10 exactly,
and money arithmetic in floats produces off-by-a-cent errors that survive most test suites.

**Timestamps.** RFC 3339 in UTC, always with an explicit offset.

**Identifiers.** Prefixed and opaque: `prod_` or `var_` followed by 24 lowercase hex
characters. Assigned by the server; never constructed by a client. A syntactically invalid id
returns `400 MALFORMED_ID`, while a well-formed id naming nothing returns `404` — so a
broken string interpolation is distinguishable from a deleted record.

## Correlation

Send `X-Request-Id` to correlate a request with your own systems, or omit it and the server
generates one. Either way the value comes back in the `X-Request-Id` **response header** on
every response, success or failure, and appears in `error.request_id`. It is on every server
log line for that request. When something goes wrong, that string is what makes the server-side
story findable.

## Pagination

Offset-based: `page` (default 1) and `limit` (default 25, maximum 100). An out-of-range
`limit` is rejected with `400` rather than silently clamped. An empty result set is `200`
with `"data": []`, never `404`. `total_pages` is `0` when `total` is `0`.

Every sort appends `id` as a tiebreaker, so paging through a sorted list cannot show the same
record twice or skip one.

## Strictness

Unknown properties in a request body, and unknown query parameters, are **rejected with 400**
rather than ignored. Most public APIs ignore them. This one does not, because
`?statuss=active` quietly returning every product is a worse outcome than a loud error that
names the unrecognised parameter.

## Errors

Branch on `error.code`, never on `error.message` — the code is the contract and the message
is prose that may be reworded at any time. `error.details` carries structured context whose
shape depends on the code.

## Authentication

Get a token from `POST /api/v1/auth/token` and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

**Catalog reads are deliberately open.** A storefront browses products without credentials.
Everything that writes — and all of locations, inventory, and pricing — requires a token.

Three roles, and permissions are what routes actually check:

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| `developer` | every read and write except admin-only actions |
| `support` | **read-only** across every domain |
| `admin` | everything |

`401` means the server does not know who you are — send credentials. `403` means it knows
exactly who you are and the answer is still no; retrying with the same token will not help. A
`403` always names the permission it wanted, in `error.details.required_permission`.
`GET /api/v1/auth/me` reports the permissions you actually hold.

This is a **development** auth flow, not an identity provider. Tokens cannot be revoked
individually and seeded passwords are published in the README. Do not deploy this where it can
be reached from the internet. Partner API keys arrive in Milestone 4.

bearerAuth.description:
A development bearer token from `POST /api/v1/auth/token`.

Send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

The token is a JWT: signed, **not encrypted**. Anyone holding it can read every claim inside it, so treat it as a credential and keep it out of anything you commit. It cannot be revoked individually — it is valid until it expires.

Catalog **reads** are deliberately unauthenticated: a storefront browses the catalog without credentials. Everything that writes, and everything under locations, inventory, and pricing, requires a token.

HealthResponse.title: HealthResponse
HealthResponse.description: Liveness. Answered from process state alone; no dependency is contacted.

status.description: Always "ok". If the process could not answer, you would get no response at all.

service.description: Service name, for when several services share a log stream.

version.description: Deployed application version. Use it to confirm an image update took effect.

environment.description: Configured APP_ENV: development, test, or production.

uptime_seconds.description: Seconds since this process started. A resetting value means it is crash-looping.

ReadinessResponse.title: ReadinessResponse
ReadinessResponse.description: Readiness. Returns 200 when the application can serve API traffic and 503 when it cannot. The body shape is identical for both, so a client parses one thing.

status.description: Overall verdict. `not_ready` is returned with HTTP 503.

checks.description: Per-dependency results, so a failure names itself.

detail.description: Human-readable explanation, useful when the check failed.

duration_ms.description: How long this check took, in milliseconds.

Product.title: Product
Product.description: A sellable item in the Acme Commerce catalog. A product carries merchandising information; the purchasable units with SKUs and prices are its variants.

id.description: Server-assigned product identifier. Always `prod_` followed by 24 lowercase hex characters. Assigned by the API; never constructed by a client.

description.description: Long-form product description. Null when none has been written.

status.description: Publication state. `draft` is not customer-visible, `active` is for sale, `archived` is retired but retained so historical orders remain meaningful.

vendor.description: Brand or supplier. Filterable via the `vendor` query parameter (case-insensitive exact match).

tags.description: Free-form labels used for merchandising. Filterable one at a time via `tag`. Always an array; an untagged product has `[]`, never null.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of creation, in UTC. Immutable.

updated_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the most recent change, in UTC. Maintained by a database trigger, so it cannot be left stale by application code that forgets to set it.

archived_at.description: When the product was archived. Non-null exactly when `status` is `archived`.

Variant.title: Variant
Variant.description: A purchasable unit of a product: one SKU, one price. Inventory and orders reference variants, not products.

product_id.description: Identifier of the product this variant belongs to.

sku.description: Stock-keeping unit. Unique across the ENTIRE catalog, not merely within one product. Creating a variant with a SKU that already exists returns 409.

title.description: Variant name, typically the option combination.

price_cents.description: Price in the smallest unit of `currency` — 12900 means CAD 129.00. An integer, never a decimal: IEEE-754 floats cannot represent 0.10 exactly, and money arithmetic in floats produces off-by-a-cent errors that survive most test suites.

compare_at_price_cents.description: Reference "was" price in minor units, used to display a markdown. Null when the variant is not on sale. Not validated against `price_cents`.

barcode.description: UPC, EAN, or ISBN. Null when unknown.

inventory_item_id.description: Reference to the inventory item that tracks stock for this variant. Always null in Milestone 1 — the Inventory API that populates it arrives in Milestone 2. Present in the contract now so the seam is visible rather than pretended away.

status.description: Variant state. Variants have no `draft`: publication is a product-level concept, so a variant of a draft product is `active` and simply not reachable by customers.

position.description: Display order within the product. `GET /products/{id}/variants` returns variants sorted by this value, then by `id` to break ties.

archived_at.description: When the variant was archived. Non-null exactly when `status` is `archived`.

Pagination.title: Pagination
Pagination.description: Offset pagination metadata, present on every collection response.

limit.description: The page size that was applied.

total.description: Total records matching the filters, across all pages.

total_pages.description: Number of pages at this `limit`. Zero when `total` is zero — not one empty page.

Error.title: Error
Error.description: The single error shape returned by every Acme Commerce API error response.

code.description: Stable machine-readable error code. Branch on this, never on `message`. The full list is documented in README.md.

message.description: Human-readable explanation, for a log or a response pane. May be reworded in any release; it is not part of the contract.

request_id.description: Correlation identifier for this request, also returned in the `X-Request-Id` response header. Quote it when reporting a problem — it is what locates the server-side log lines.

details.description: Optional structured context. Its shape depends on `code`: `VALIDATION_ERROR` carries a `fields` array, `MALFORMED_ID` carries `expected_pattern`, `SKU_ALREADY_EXISTS` carries the conflicting `sku`.

ProductCreate.title: ProductCreate
ProductCreate.description: Body for creating a product. Unknown properties are REJECTED with 400 rather than ignored — a silently-dropped `titel` is a typo that ships to production believing it worked.

status.description: Optional. Defaults to `draft`, so a new product is not accidentally live.

tags.description: Optional labels. Defaults to an empty array.

example.title: Riverbend Packable Rain Jacket
example.description: A 2.5-layer shell that stuffs into its own pocket.

ProductUpdate.title: ProductUpdate
ProductUpdate.description: Partial update. Only the properties you send are changed. An omitted property is left alone; an explicit null clears a nullable property. Those are genuinely different operations, which is the whole reason PATCH exists rather than PUT. An empty body is rejected with 400 — it is far more often a client bug than a deliberate no-op.

description.description: New description. Send null to clear it.

status.description: New publication state. Setting `archived` here is equivalent to calling DELETE; moving away from `archived` un-archives the product and clears `archived_at`.

vendor.description: New vendor. Send null to clear it.

product_type.description: New product type. Send null to clear it.

tags.description: Replaces the entire tag array. This is not a merge; send the full list.

VariantCreate.title: VariantCreate
VariantCreate.description: Body for creating a variant. The parent product is taken from the URL path, not the body, so the two cannot disagree.

sku.description: Required. Must be unique across the entire catalog.

price_cents.description: Required. Price in minor units. Must be a non-negative integer.

compare_at_price_cents.description: Optional reference price in minor units.

currency.description: Optional ISO 4217 code. Defaults to CAD.

position.description: Optional display order. Defaults to one past the current highest position.

VariantUpdate.title: VariantUpdate
VariantUpdate.description: Partial update of a variant. Same omitted-versus-null semantics as ProductUpdate.

sku.description: New SKU. Still subject to global uniqueness.

compare_at_price_cents.description: New reference price. Send null to remove the markdown.

barcode.description: New barcode. Send null to clear it.

status.description: New variant state. `archived` is equivalent to DELETE.

ProductListResponse.title: ProductListResponse
ProductListResponse.description: A page of products plus the pagination metadata needed to fetch the rest.

data.description: The requested page of products. Empty when nothing matches.

VariantListResponse.title: VariantListResponse
VariantListResponse.description: Every variant belonging to one product, unpaginated.

data.description: All variants of the product, ordered by `position` then `id`. This sub-collection is not paginated: a product has tens of variants, not thousands. The response is capped at 250.

TokenRequest.title: TokenRequest
TokenRequest.description: Credentials exchanged for a bearer token.

email.description: Email address of a development user. Case-insensitive.

password.description: The user's password. Seeded development users share one; see the README.

Identity.title: Identity
Identity.description: The authenticated caller, as the server currently understands them.

id.description: User identifier. Appears as the `sub` claim in the token.

role.description: Internal role. Determines the permission set; permissions are derived from the role at request time, never carried inside the token.

permissions.description: Every permission this role holds. What a 403 is checked against.

token_expires_at.description: When the presented token stops being accepted.

TokenResponse.title: TokenResponse
TokenResponse.description: A newly issued development bearer token, with the identity it represents.

access_token.description: A JWT. Send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It is signed, not encrypted — anyone holding it can read every claim inside it, so treat it as a credential.

IdentityResponse.title: IdentityResponse
IdentityResponse.description: The identity behind the presented token.

Location.title: Location
Location.description: A place where inventory is held.

type.description: Kind of location. `warehouse` fulfils orders, `retail` is a physical store, `virtual` covers dropship and in-transit stock that has no address.

address_line1.description: Street address. Null for a virtual location.

is_active.description: Whether the location is in use. Locations are never deleted — inventory history references them — so retiring one means setting this to false.

LocationCreate.title: LocationCreate
LocationCreate.description: Body for creating an inventory location.

type.description: Kind of location. `warehouse` fulfils orders, `retail` is a physical store, `virtual` covers dropship and in-transit stock that has no address.

LocationUpdate.title: LocationUpdate
LocationUpdate.description: Partial update. Omitted properties are unchanged; explicit null clears one.

type.description: Kind of location. `warehouse` fulfils orders, `retail` is a physical store, `virtual` covers dropship and in-transit stock that has no address.

address_line1.description: New street address; null clears it.

address_line2.description: New unit or suite; null clears it.

postal_code.description: New postal code; null clears it.

country.description: New ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code; null clears it.

is_active.description: Set false to retire the location without deleting it.

LocationListResponse.title: LocationListResponse
LocationListResponse.description: A page of locations with pagination metadata.

InventoryLevel.title: InventoryLevel
InventoryLevel.description: Stock for one SKU at one location.

sku.description: The SKU this level is for.

location_name.description: Location name, so a response is readable without a second call.

available.description: What can still be reserved or sold: `on_hand - reserved`. **Computed, never stored** — a third stored number is the first thing to disagree with the other two.

SkuInventory.title: SkuInventory
SkuInventory.description: Availability for one SKU across every location.

tracked.description: Whether stock is tracked for this SKU.

locations.description: Per-location breakdown. A location with no stock row for this SKU is absent, not zero.

InventoryAdjustment.title: InventoryAdjustment
InventoryAdjustment.description: One entry in the append-only stock audit log.

reason.description: Why the stock moved. A closed set so history can be grouped.

reference.description: Free-text link to a PO, order, or ticket.

actor.description: Who did it — taken from the bearer token, never from the body.

status.description: Lifecycle state. `expired` is reported as soon as `expires_at` passes, whether or not the stock has been swept back yet.

reference.description: Free-text link to a cart or order.

expires_at.description: After this, the hold lapses and the stock returns.

released_at.description: When it was released or expired. Null while active.

AdjustmentRequest.title: AdjustmentRequest
AdjustmentRequest.description: Increase, decrease, or correct stock at one location.

quantity_delta.description: Signed change. Positive adds, negative removes. Zero is rejected — an adjustment that changes nothing is a client bug, not a no-op worth recording.

reason.description: Required. Closed set so the audit log can be grouped and reported on.

reference.description: Optional PO number, order id, or ticket.

ReservationRequest.title: ReservationRequest
ReservationRequest.description: Hold stock for a pending transaction.

location_id.description: Which location to hold stock at.

quantity.description: Units to hold. Must be positive.

ttl_seconds.description: How long the hold lasts. Defaults to 15 minutes.

AdjustmentResponse.title: AdjustmentResponse
AdjustmentResponse.description: The adjustment recorded, and the level it produced.

level.description: The resulting level, so no follow-up read is needed.

data.description: A page of audit-log entries, newest first.

PriceAdjustment.title: PriceAdjustment
PriceAdjustment.description: One pricing rule and what it did.

type.description: Rule kind: sale, customer_group, quantity_break, or partner.

description.description: Human-readable rule name, safe to show a customer.

amount_cents.description: Signed change this rule made to the running subtotal, in minor units. Negative is a discount. Zero when `applied` is false.

applied.description: Whether the rule actually changed the price.

skipped_reason.description: Why the rule did not apply. Null when it did. Rules that were considered and skipped are reported deliberately — "the wholesale discount exists and you did not get it because you sent no customer_id" is the answer a support engineer needs.

PriceQuote.title: PriceQuote
PriceQuote.description: An effective price with its full derivation. Rules apply in ascending priority, each against the running subtotal rather than the base price — so two 10% discounts compound to 19%, not 20%. Each step rounds to a whole minor unit, half away from zero.

currency.description: ISO 4217 code. This API does not convert currencies.

quantity.description: Quantity the quote was calculated for.

base_price_cents.description: The variant list price before any rule.

adjustments.description: Every rule considered, in the order applied (ascending priority). Applied and skipped rules are both present.

effective_unit_price_cents.description: Price for one unit after every applicable rule. Equals `base_price_cents` plus the sum of `amount_cents` — the breakdown always reconciles exactly.

applied_rule_ids.description: Just the rules that applied, for logging or audit.

PriceQuoteResponse.title: PriceQuoteResponse
PriceQuoteResponse.description: An effective price and how it was reached.

get.description:
Reports that the process is running and able to answer HTTP. **It does not contact
PostgreSQL**, and it does not fail when the database is down.

That is the whole distinction between liveness and readiness, and getting it wrong
is a classic outage amplifier: if a liveness probe fails during a database blip, the
orchestrator restarts every application container, and now you have a database
outage plus a thundering herd of cold starts. Liveness answers "should this process
be killed and replaced?" — a database outage is not a reason to kill this process.

Use this for a Docker HEALTHCHECK. Use `/ready` to decide whether to send traffic.

Reports whether the application can serve API traffic right now. Three checks:

1. **configuration** — required settings were present and valid at startup. This one
   cannot realistically fail here, because invalid configuration prevents the process
   from starting at all. It is reported so the probe output is a complete picture.
2. **database** — a live round trip to PostgreSQL. Catches a wrong host, a wrong
   password, a firewall, and a stopped database container.
3. **migrations** — whether every migration on disk has been applied. A container
   running new code against an old schema is a specific, common, and confusing
   failure; it is worth its own check.

Returns `200` when all three pass and `503` when any fails, with the same body shape
either way. Each check reports its own duration, so "the database is slow" and "the
database is unreachable" look different.

Outside production the body also names the database being checked, with the password
removed — that is usually the fastest way to discover a container is pointed at the
wrong host.

200.description: Every check passed; the application can serve traffic.

503.description: At least one check failed. Inspect `checks` to see which.

get.description:
Returns the OpenAPI 3.1 document describing this API.

It is generated from the same JSON Schema objects that validate incoming requests and
serialize outgoing responses, so it cannot describe a request shape the server would
reject or a response field the server would strip.

What that guarantee does NOT cover: whether a `description` is accurate, whether an
`example` is current, or whether an operation is missing entirely. Those need review
and linting, not generation.

Import this URL into Postman to generate a collection skeleton.

Returns a page of products with pagination metadata.

**No implicit filtering.** With no `status` parameter, products of every status are
returned, archived ones included. This API applies no hidden default filter: the result
set is fully determined by the query string. Most catalog APIs hide archived records;
this one does not, so that DELETE is observable as a state change rather than as a
disappearance.

Filters combine with AND. An empty result is `200` with `"data": []`, never `404` —
an empty collection is a successful answer to a well-formed question. A page past the
end is also `200` with an empty array.

**Unknown query parameters are rejected with 400**, not ignored. `?statuss=active`
silently returning every product is a worse outcome than a loud error.

Ordering always ends with `id` as a tiebreaker, so paging through a sorted list cannot
show the same record twice.

Every response carries an `X-Request-Id` header.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: One-based page number. Requesting a page past the end returns an empty `data` array with 200, not 404.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Records per page. Default 25, maximum 100. A larger value is rejected with 400 rather than silently clamped, so a client asking for 1000 learns that it cannot have 1000.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Filter by publication state. NOTE: with no `status` filter, products of ALL statuses are returned, archived included. This API applies no hidden default filter — the result set is fully determined by the query string.

parameters.name: vendor
parameters.description: Filter by vendor. Case-insensitive EXACT match, not a prefix or substring.

parameters.name: product_type
parameters.description: Filter by product type. Case-insensitive exact match.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: Filter to products carrying this tag. Case-sensitive exact match on an array element. One tag per request in this version.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring search across `title`, `description`, and `vendor`. Does not search variant SKUs. Combines with the filters using AND.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Field to sort by. Restricted to this allowlist; any other value returns 400 with the permitted values in `error.details.allowed`. `id` is always appended as a tiebreaker so paging is stable across requests.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Sort direction. Applies to the tiebreaker too.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Optional caller-supplied correlation id, echoed back in the X-Request-Id response header and included in structured errors. When absent or not matching this pattern, the server generates one. Supplying your own lets you correlate a request across your system and ours.

400.description: The request is malformed. `error.code` is VALIDATION_ERROR, MALFORMED_ID, or INVALID_JSON.

500.description: An unexpected server error. `error.request_id` identifies the failure in the server logs.

503.description: The database is unreachable. Safe to retry; see the Retry-After header.

post.description:
Creates a product. The identifier, timestamps, and archive state are assigned by the
server and cannot be supplied.

A new product defaults to `draft` status so that creating one does not accidentally
publish it.

Unknown body properties are rejected with `400` rather than ignored, so a misspelled
field is visible immediately instead of shipping to production believing it worked.

Responds `201` with a `Location` header pointing at the new product.

get.description:
Returns one product by identifier.

Two different failures are deliberately distinguished. A syntactically invalid id
such as `prod_undefined` returns `400 MALFORMED_ID`, because that is a client bug.
A well-formed id that names nothing returns `404 PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND`. Collapsing both
into 404 — as many APIs do — leaves the caller unable to tell a broken string
interpolation from a deleted record.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description: Product identifier as returned by the API.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Optional caller-supplied correlation id, echoed back in the X-Request-Id response header and included in structured errors. When absent or not matching this pattern, the server generates one. Supplying your own lets you correlate a request across your system and ours.

400.description: The request is malformed. `error.code` is VALIDATION_ERROR, MALFORMED_ID, or INVALID_JSON.

404.description: No product exists with that identifier (`PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND`).

500.description: An unexpected server error. `error.request_id` identifies the failure in the server logs.

503.description: The database is unreachable. Safe to retry; see the Retry-After header.

patch.description:
Updates only the properties present in the body.

Omitting a property leaves it unchanged; sending an explicit `null` clears a
nullable property. Those are different operations, and being able to express both
is the reason this is PATCH rather than PUT.

`tags` is replaced wholesale, not merged — send the complete list you want.

An empty body returns `400`: it is far more often a client bug than a deliberate
no-op. Setting `status` to `archived` here is equivalent to calling DELETE, and
moving it away from `archived` un-archives the product and its variants.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description: Product identifier as returned by the API.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Optional caller-supplied correlation id, echoed back in the X-Request-Id response header and included in structured errors. When absent or not matching this pattern, the server generates one. Supplying your own lets you correlate a request across your system and ours.

400.description: The request is malformed. `error.code` is VALIDATION_ERROR, MALFORMED_ID, or INVALID_JSON.

401.description: Missing, malformed, invalid, or expired bearer token.

404.description: No product exists with that identifier (`PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND`).

500.description: An unexpected server error. `error.request_id` identifies the failure in the server logs.

503.description: The database is unreachable. Safe to retry; see the Retry-After header.

delete.description:
**Archives the product; it is not destroyed.** Status becomes `archived`,
`archived_at` is set, and all of its variants are archived with it.

Catalog records are referenced by historical orders. Hard-deleting a variant that a
two-year-old order points at destroys that order's meaning, so retiring a product
is a state change rather than a deletion. Archived products remain retrievable and
still appear in `GET /products` unless you filter them out.

Responds `200` with the archived product rather than `204 No Content`, so the state
transition is visible in the response you are already looking at.

**Idempotent.** Archiving an already-archived product returns `200` again, not a
conflict — repeating a delete after a network timeout is not an error.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description: Product identifier as returned by the API.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Optional caller-supplied correlation id, echoed back in the X-Request-Id response header and included in structured errors. When absent or not matching this pattern, the server generates one. Supplying your own lets you correlate a request across your system and ours.

200.description: The archived product. Returned for a repeat call too.

400.description: The request is malformed. `error.code` is VALIDATION_ERROR, MALFORMED_ID, or INVALID_JSON.

401.description: Missing, malformed, invalid, or expired bearer token.

404.description: No product exists with that identifier (`PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND`).

500.description: An unexpected server error. `error.request_id` identifies the failure in the server logs.

503.description: The database is unreachable. Safe to retry; see the Retry-After header.

get.description:
Returns every variant of the product, ordered by `position` then `id`.

Deliberately **not paginated**: a product has tens of variants, not thousands, and
forcing a caller to page through a size run would be pointless ceremony. The
response is capped at 250 variants, which is documented rather than assumed.

Because it is not a paginated collection, the response has no `pagination` object —
the one place in this API where a collection differs in shape, and it is called out
here so that a governance review can confirm the reason rather than flag an
inconsistency.

An unknown product returns `404`, not an empty list: "this product has no variants"
and "this product does not exist" are different facts.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description: Product identifier as returned by the API.

parameters.name: x-request-id
parameters.description: Optional caller-supplied correlation id, echoed back in the X-Request-Id response header and included in structured errors. When absent or not matching this pattern, the server generates one. Supplying your own lets you correlate a request across your system and ours.

post.description:
Adds a variant to the product named in the path. The parent is taken from the URL,
not the body, so the two cannot disagree.

`sku` must be unique across the ENTIRE catalog, not merely within this product. A
duplicate returns `409 SKU_ALREADY_EXISTS` with the conflicting variant id in
`error.details`. Uniqueness is enforced by a database constraint rather than by a
lookup before insert, because two concurrent requests can both pass a lookup.

`position` defaults to one past the current highest.

Responds `201` with a `Location` header.

post.summary: Exchange credentials for a bearer token
post.description:
Issues a signed JWT for a known development user.

**This is a development authentication flow, not an identity provider.** There is no
registration, password reset, email verification, refresh token, or session. It exists
so that bearer tokens, roles, permissions, and expiry have something real to attach to.
Do not model a production auth system on it.

**The token is signed, not encrypted.** Decode the middle segment and you can read every
claim — that is normal and expected. The signature makes the claims tamper-evident, not
secret. Nothing sensitive is put inside it.

**Tokens cannot be revoked.** A stateless token is valid until it expires; the only
global lever is rotating the signing secret. That is why the lifetime is short. A
deactivated user *is* rejected immediately, because the account is re-read on every
request rather than trusted from the token.

Unknown email, wrong password, and deactivated account all return the identical
`401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, in comparable time. Distinguishing them would let this
endpoint be used to discover which accounts exist.

Rate limited per client IP — it is unauthenticated and runs a deliberately expensive
password hash on every call.

Returns the identity behind the presented token, including the full permission set
and when the token expires.

The most useful endpoint in the API while you are debugging a `403`: it answers
"who does the server think I am, and what am I allowed to do" without guessing.

Permissions are resolved from the user's **current** role, not from the `role` claim
in the token. Change someone's role and it takes effect on their next request rather
than when their token expires.

Paginated stock levels across SKUs and locations.

`available` is `on_hand - reserved`, **computed at read time**. There is no stored
availability column, because a third stored number is the first thing to disagree
with the other two.

`?available_below=5` is the low-stock query — it filters on the computed value, not
on `on_hand`, so stock that is physically present but entirely reserved correctly
counts as unavailable.

The log is **append-only**: entries are never updated and never deleted. That is what
makes it an audit log rather than a cache of current belief — the sum of the deltas
for a SKU and location reconciles with its `on_hand`.

Note that seeded fixture stock has no history. Fabricating adjustments for data that
was never adjusted would make the log a worse record.

post.summary: Reserve stock for a pending transaction
post.description:
Holds stock so it cannot be sold twice while a transaction is in flight.

**Two callers cannot both reserve the last unit.** The hold is applied by attempting
the update and letting a database constraint arbitrate, not by reading availability
and then writing. A read-check-write has a race window that only appears under
concurrency — which is to say, only in production. Losing that race returns
`409 INVENTORY_INSUFFICIENT` with the authoritative available quantity.

Reservations expire (15 minutes by default). Expired holds are swept back inside the
next reservation attempt for the same SKU and location, so lapsed stock frees itself
on next use rather than needing a scheduler.

**Idempotent.** Releasing an already-released reservation returns `200` with it
unchanged, for the same reason archiving a product twice does: "make sure this is

Releasing an **expired** reservation is different and returns `409` — its stock was
already reclaimed, so succeeding silently would let you believe you had returned
stock you had not.

Stock for a single SKU across every location, with network-wide totals.

**The path parameter is a SKU, not an opaque id** — the one place in this API where a
human-meaningful natural key sits in a path, because that is how people refer to
inventory. The tradeoff: renaming a SKU changes the URL, which an opaque id would
have insulated you from.

A location with no stock row for this SKU is absent from `locations` rather than
reported as zero. Never stocked there and stocked-but-empty are different facts.

get.summary: Calculate the effective price for a SKU
get.description:
Returns the price **and the derivation**, not just a number.

The response lists every rule considered, in the order applied, with the amount each
contributed — and the ones that did **not** apply, with the reason. That last part is
the difference between an API a support engineer can answer a question with and one
that produces a figure nobody can explain.

**Order and compounding.** Rules apply in ascending `priority`, each against the
running subtotal rather than the base price. Two 10% discounts therefore compound to
19%, not 20%. A business decision, stated rather than implied.

**Rounding.** Each step rounds to a whole minor unit, half away from zero. Each
reported `amount_cents` is defined as the difference between the subtotal before and
after, so the adjustments always sum exactly to `effective_unit_price_cents`.

Requires `pricing:read` because `?customer_id=` returns customer-specific pricing, and
commercial terms are not public.

parameters.name: currency
parameters.description: Assert the currency you expect. Mismatching the price's own currency returns 404 rather than converting — a wrong exchange rate silently applied is worse than a refusal.
